opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to the nature of the problem. A lot of people come to AI risk through the technical lens, asking how we make sure a system does what we intend. That's crucial work. But many of the hardest challenges with advanced AI aren't purely technical. They're about how institutions behave, how states compete, how companies respond to incentives, how power gets distributed, and how societies coordinate when the stakes are high and trust is low.

Those are classic social science questions. Political scientists have studied arms races, bargaining failures, and why rational actors end up in outcomes nobody wants. Economists think about market structure, concentration, and labor displacement. Sociologists and historians look at how transformative technologies reshaped societies before. International relations scholars study verification, treaties, and building trust between rivals. All of that bears directly on whether the transition to advanced AI goes well.

Yet when I started working in this area, there were very few people bringing that expertise to bear seriously. The field was dominated by computer scientists and philosophers, both essential, but missing a large chunk of relevant knowledge. You'd see proposals that sounded reasonable in the abstract but didn't grapple with political feasibility, institutional dynamics, or how actors actually behave under competitive pressure.

There's also the fact that even if we solve the technical alignment problem perfectly, we still face a governance problem: aligned with whom, deployed by whom, under what constraints? A world where a highly capable, perfectly controllable AI is held by a small group with no accountability is not obviously safe. Navigating that requires understanding legitimacy, institutional design, and collective decision-making.

So my view has been that social scientists have an enormous amount to contribute, and the talent gap is real. We need people who can bring rigorous empirical and theoretical tools to these questions, and who are willing to engage seriously with the technology rather than treating it as just another policy domain. That combination is rare, and it's one of the highest-leverage places someone can work right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI’s effects on institutions, states, companies, power, markets, labor, and society, then explains that addressing these challenges calls for expertise from several social science fields.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it starts from an observation about what the hard problems in AI governance actually are. When people first think about AI safety or AI governance, the mind naturally goes to the technical side: alignment, interpretability, how do we make sure the system does what we want. And those problems are real and important. But if you step back and ask what determines whether the transition to advanced AI goes well, a huge share of the answer is about how humans and institutions respond. It's about states competing with one another, about firms racing or cooperating, about how norms form, about how publics perceive risk, about what kinds of agreements are actually enforceable.

Those are fundamentally social science questions. They're questions that political scientists, economists, historians, sociologists, legal scholars have been thinking about for a long time, in other domains. Arms control, nuclear strategy, the regulation of general-purpose technologies like electricity or the internet, international cooperation on things like climate. There's a rich body of knowledge there about why cooperation succeeds or fails, about how verification regimes get built, about how structural incentives shape behavior even when individual actors have good intentions.

And what I noticed, and what motivated a lot of my own work, is that the AI community has historically been dominated by people with a computer science or technical background. Which makes sense, that's where the technology comes from. But it means the governance conversation often gets conducted by people who are, in a sense, reinventing the wheel. They'll arrive at ideas about racing dynamics or collective action problems from first principles, which is admirable, but there's a whole literature that could accelerate that thinking and also warn about the failure modes we've already seen historically.

So the gap, as I see it, is that there are relatively few people who have both a deep understanding of the technology and its trajectory, and real fluency in these social science frameworks. If you're an international relations scholar, you probably haven't been following the frontier of machine learning. And if you're a machine learning researcher, you probably haven't thought carefully about, say, the conditions under which great powers can credibly commit to restraint. Bridging that is hard, and it's a relatively small community doing it.

I'd also add that it's not just about importing existing theories. Advanced AI may be genuinely novel in some respects, so part of the work is figuring out where the analogies hold and where they break down. That requires people who can take social science seriously as a method, as a way of asking structured questions and testing them, rather than just reaching for the nearest historical comparison. So when I say it's a gap, I mean both that we need more people with the training, and that we need them to actually engage deeply with the specifics of AI rather than treating it as just another technology.

r001.rationale: The response says advanced AI’s outcomes depend heavily on how humans and institutions respond across states, firms, norms, publics, and agreements, and identifies these as social science questions.

astra-6.text:
Well, AI governance is fundamentally about how people and institutions respond to this technology. Technical expertise is essential for understanding what AI systems can do, but it doesn’t by itself tell you how governments will compete, how firms will respond to regulation, or what kinds of agreements will be credible.

For example, people often talk about an AI arms race. But that’s really the beginning of a set of questions: What are the actors competing over? How much do they know about one another’s capabilities? When does competition lead them to cut corners on safety? And what arrangements could reduce those pressures? Those are questions for political science, economics, and other social sciences.

I think there’s a gap both in bringing that expertise into AI discussions and in getting social scientists to engage deeply with the technology. You need both. Otherwise, you risk proposing policies that sound technically sensible but depend on unrealistic assumptions about how institutions behave.

And these questions are difficult. We shouldn’t expect social science to give us precise predictions about the future. But it can help us identify the assumptions we’re making, distinguish plausible scenarios, and design policies that work under a wider range of conditions.

r001.rationale: The response links AI governance to how people and institutions respond, then gives examples involving governments, firms, regulation, competition, and agreements to explain why social science expertise is needed.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, AI governance is fundamentally about how people and institutions respond to a powerful new technology. Technical expertise is essential, but it doesn’t by itself tell us how governments will compete, what firms have incentives to do, or which kinds of agreements will actually hold up under pressure. Those are social science questions.

For example, suppose we identify a safety measure that we’d like every leading AI developer to adopt. We still need to understand whether adopting it puts a firm at a competitive disadvantage, whether others can verify compliance, and what institutions could make cooperation sustainable. Identifying a technically desirable outcome is only part of the problem; we also need to understand how to get there.

So I think there’s a lot of room for people with expertise in political science, economics, sociology, and related fields to contribute. The challenge is to bring that expertise into close contact with an understanding of AI, so that we’re asking questions that matter for the actual decisions people face.

r001.rationale: The response connects AI governance to how people, governments, firms, and institutions respond to a powerful technology, and says expertise across social science fields is needed to understand those effects.
